Q: Is it possible to create service/GUI to be able to monitor rate of communication and provide evaluation between servers and hardware? A:

This sounds like a job for telemetry, specifically metrics. If your services don't already, modify them to support exporting these metrics, collect them in a central place and then visualize them using a dashboard like Grafana. You can do this directly in .NET using the metrics API, look at creating metrics, and then look at collecting metrics

I'd recommend exporting them to a Prometheus and then using Grafana to visualize these metrics.

P.S. Grafana also has built in alerting that can notify you (or anyone else) if something's going wrong.

Q: Is there a 128 bit integer in gcc? A:

Starting with C23, you can use the _BitInt(128) and unsigned _BitInt(128) types for signed and unsigned 128-bit integers, respectively. However, these types are not mandatory; they only exist if BITINT_MAXWIDTH >= 128. In practice, if __int128 exists, _BitInt(128) is also available. There are architectures (like 32-bit GCC targets) where neither is available, so you need to use a third-party library to emulate 128-bit integers.

_BitInt(128) has a number of advantages over __int128:

  • _BitInt(128) is a standard feature, not a compiler extension like __int128.
  • __int128 is excessively aligned for a lot of use cases (to 16 bytes). This can create a lot of padding between members when putting it into a struct. The underlying CPU instructions on 64-bit architectures also don't require 128-bit memory alignment, but operate on pairs of registers.
  • _BitInt(128) could become portable to C++ in the future. P3666 "Bit-precise integers" proposes _BitInt for C++29.

At the time of writing, Clang has has full support for _BitInt, GCC only supports it on some architectures (namely on those where __int128 is already available), and MSVC doesn't support _BitInt at all; see https://cppstat.dev/?search=bitint.

It's also worth noting that if you just need to do 64-by-64-to-128-bit multiplication (like the question states), you don't really need 128-bit integers. You can write a function that gets you the low and high bits of a multiplication; see Getting the high part of 64 bit integer multiplication.

Q: How do I sort a dictionary by key? A:

For the way how question is formulated, the most answers here are answering it correctly.

However, considering how the things should be really done, taking to account decades and decades of computer science, it comes to my total suprise that there is actually only one answer here (from GrantJ user) suggesting usage of sorted associative containers (sortedcontainers) which sorts elements based on key at their insertions point.

That will avoid massive performance impact per each calling of sorted(...) (at minimum O(N*log(N)), where N is the number of elements (logically, this applies for all such solutions here which suggest to use the sorted(...)). Take to account that for all such solutions, the sorted(...) will need to be called every time when collection needs to be accessed as sorted AFTER it was modified by adding/removing elements ...
